newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronaut returns to earth.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronaut returns to earth.

text.p: U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger returned home aboard the space shuttle Atlantis on Saturday after a tour of duty aboard Russia's troubled Mir space station.

The winged spaceship, closely followed by a NASA weather plane, swooped out of a partly cloudy sky and touched down at 9:27 a.m. EDT (1327 GMT) on the three-mile (5-km) runway at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
"We'd like to offer congratulations on a flawless flight and a special welcome home for Jerry," mission control's Dominic Gorie radioed as the shuttle came to a halt.
"Feeling great and good to be home," replied Linenger from a cushioned reclining seat on the shuttle's lower deck.
It was the first time since blasting off in January that he had felt the pull of gravity.
His four-month stay on Mir was marred by a serious fire, life support problems and a near collision with an unmanned cargo craft.
The highlight of the mission came in April when Linenger and his Russian commander, Vasily Tsibliev, stepped outside on a spacewalk, the first by an American from Mir.

Atlantis, which blasted off on May 15, spent five days docked at the Russian orbital outpost. It left behind Linnenger's replacement, British-born astronaut Michael Foale, and nearly two tonnes of supplies and equipment.
Foale, the fifth U.S. astronaut to live and work on Mir, is to return to Earth in September.

The shuttle's touchdown was delayed 90 minutes by cloudy skies at the Florida spaceport. Flight controllers in Houston watched the weather until the last minute before giving the shuttle permission to land.

The astronauts were expected to leave the shuttle about an hour after touchdown. Linenger, a 42-year-old medical doctor and navy captain, said he was determined to walk off the shuttle after its landing, despite NASA's preference for him to be carried off.
During his stay on Mir, Linenger, who listed marathon running and ocean swimming among his hobbies, was to run daily for two hours on a treadmill to keep up his strength.
Although that exercise programme was disrupted by the problems aboard Mir, NASA did not expect any complications after Linenger's return to earth.
Long duration space flights, away from the pull of gravity, cause bones to weaken and muscles to waste away.
A team of doctors and nurses was standing by in a special vehicle to examine the former Mir resident.
Linenger's 132-day stay in space was the second-longest mission for an American astronaut. Shannon Lucid set the U.S. record with a 188-day stay on Mir in 1996.
Linenger said he expected to feel "pure elation" when he is reunited with his 18-month old son, John, and his wife, Kathryn, who is pregnant with their second child.
